# Decision trees and random forests {#sec-ch-mla-trees}

> *"Random forests are a combination of tree predictors such that each tree

## Learning objectives
By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

- control a tree's complexity by limiting its growth or by **cost-complexity

- explain why trees have high **variance**, **prove** the variance formula

- build **random forests**, explain how feature subsampling decorrelates the

:::

## Topics covered
Decision trees; the bias–variance trade-off; bagging to reduce variance;

## Intuition: twenty questions {#sec-tree-intuition}

In the game of twenty questions, one player thinks of an object and the other
identifies it by yes/no questions. A good player asks first the question that
splits the remaining possibilities most evenly, then adapts the next question
to the answer. A **decision tree** plays this game with data: "is the weight
below 40 g?", then, depending on the answer, "is the diameter below 25 mm?",
and so on, until the examples that reach a **leaf** mostly share a class. The
learned tree is a set of nested rules that a person can read, check and
apply with pen and paper.

Trees are flexible — they can carve the feature space into many rectangles —
and that is their weakness: a slightly different training sample can give a
very different tree. Averaging many trees grown on perturbed versions of the
data keeps the flexibility and removes much of the instability. That is
**bagging**, and with an extra dose of randomness, the **random forest** — for
two decades one of the most reliable off-the-shelf methods for tabular data.

## Decision trees {#sec-tree-trees}

A (binary) decision tree partitions the feature space by **axis-aligned
splits**: each internal node tests $x_j \le t$ for one feature $j$ and a
threshold $t$, sending the example left or right; each leaf predicts the
majority class (classification) or the mean target (regression) of the
training examples that reach it. Trees are grown **greedily**, top-down: at
each node, choose the split that most reduces an **impurity** measure of the
labels, then recurse on the two children, until a stopping rule. This is the
CART algorithm of Breiman, Friedman, Olshen and Stone [@breiman1984]; Quinlan's
ID3 and C4.5 are close relatives using entropy [@quinlan1986; @quinlan1993].

### Impurity

For a node whose examples have class proportions $p = (p_1, \dots, p_K)$:

| Impurity | Formula | Pure node | Uniform ($p_k = 1/K$) |
|---|---|---|---|
| misclassification | $1 - \max_kp_k$ | 0 | $1 - 1/K$ |
| **Gini** | $\sum_kp_k(1 - p_k) = 1 - \sum_kp_k^2$ | 0 | $1 - 1/K$ |
| **entropy** | $-\sum_kp_k\log_2p_k$ | 0 | $\log_2K$ |

: Impurity measures (scikit-learn's `criterion="gini"`, `"entropy"` or `"log_loss"`) {#tbl-tree-impurity}

The Gini impurity is the probability that two examples drawn at random from
the node (with replacement) have different classes; the entropy is the
average number of bits needed to encode the class of an example of the node
[@shannon1948]. Splitting a node $S$ of $n$ examples into $S_L$ and $S_R$ is
scored by the **impurity decrease**
$$
\Delta = I(S) - \frac{n_L}{n}I(S_L) - \frac{n_R}{n}I(S_R),
$$ {#eq-tree-gain}
called **information gain** when $I$ is the entropy.

::: {#thm-tree-concave}
## Splitting never increases a concave impurity
Let $I$ be a concave function of the class proportions. For every split,
$\Delta \ge 0$. Gini and entropy are strictly concave, so $\Delta = 0$ only
when both children have the same proportions as the parent.
:::

*In one line:* the parent's proportions are the weighted average of the
children's, and a concave function of an average is at least the average of
the function — so the weighted impurity of the children can only be lower.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @thm-tree-concave
With $p^L, p^R$ the children's proportions, the parent's are $p =
\frac{n_L}{n}p^L + \frac{n_R}{n}p^R$ (count the class-$k$ examples on both
sides). By concavity, $I(p) \ge \frac{n_L}{n}I(p^L) + \frac{n_R}{n}I(p^R)$,
i.e. $\Delta \ge 0$, with equality for a strictly concave $I$ only if $p^L =
p^R$. Gini: $1 - \lVert p\rVert^2$ is strictly concave because $\lVert
p\rVert^2$ is strictly convex. Entropy: $-p\log p$ has second derivative
$-1/(p\ln2) < 0$, and a sum of strictly concave functions of separate
coordinates is strictly concave. $\blacksquare$ The misclassification
impurity is concave but piecewise linear: many useful splits leave it
unchanged, which is why it is a poor criterion for growing trees
[@hastie2009, §9.2.3] (@exr-mla7-trees-easy).
:::

::: {#exm-tree-hand}
## Choosing a split by hand
A node holds 10 examples, 6 of class A and 4 of class B: Gini $1 - 0.6^2 -
0.4^2 = 0.48$. Candidate split 1 sends 5 A and 1 B left, 1 A and 3 B right:
Gini left $1 - (5/6)^2 - (1/6)^2 \approx 0.278$, right $1 - (1/4)^2 - (3/4)^2 =
0.375$, weighted $0.6\cdot0.278 + 0.4\cdot0.375 \approx 0.317$, decrease $0.163$.
Candidate 2 sends 3 A and 0 B left, 3 A and 4 B right: left $0$, right $1 -
(3/7)^2 - (4/7)^2 \approx 0.490$, weighted $0.7\cdot0.490 = 0.343$, decrease
$0.137$. Split 1 is chosen.
:::

For **regression** the impurity of a node is the mean squared deviation of
its targets from their mean: the mean is the constant with the smallest
squared error (@thm-regression-function, applied to the empirical
distribution of the node), and @eq-tree-gain with this impurity is the
reduction of the residual sum of squares.

### Finding the best split

For one feature, sort the node's examples by its value; the candidate
thresholds are the midpoints between consecutive distinct values. Sweeping
left to right, the class counts on each side are updated by one example at a
time, so all candidates are scored in $O(n)$ after an $O(n\log n)$ sort. Over
$d$ features, a node costs $O(dn\log n)$.

::: {#4422a2dd .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, export_text

def gini(counts):
    p = counts / counts.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    return 1 - (p ** 2).sum(axis=-1)

def best_split(X, y, classes):
    """Best (feature, threshold, decrease) by Gini, scanning sorted values once per feature."""
    n = len(y)
    parent = gini(np.array([np.sum(y == c) for c in classes], float))
    best = (None, None, 0.0)
    Y = (y[:, None] == classes[None, :]).astype(float)           # one-hot labels
    for j in range(X.shape[1]):
        order = np.argsort(X[:, j], kind="stable")
        xs, Ys = X[order, j], Y[order]
        left = np.cumsum(Ys, axis=0)[:-1]                         # counts left of each cut position
        right = Ys.sum(0) - left
        nl = np.arange(1, n)[:, None]
        valid = xs[1:] > xs[:-1]                                  # cut only between distinct values
        dec = parent - (nl[:, 0] / n) * gini(left) - ((n - nl[:, 0]) / n) * gini(right)
        dec[~valid] = -np.inf
        i = int(np.argmax(dec))
        if dec[i] > best[2] + 1e-12:
            best = (j, (xs[i] + xs[i + 1]) / 2, dec[i])
    return best

def grow(X, y, classes, depth, max_depth):
    """A depth-limited CART tree as nested dicts."""
    counts = np.array([np.sum(y == c) for c in classes])
    j, t, dec = best_split(X, y, classes) if depth < max_depth and len(np.unique(y)) > 1 else (None, None, 0)
    if j is None:
        return {"leaf": classes[np.argmax(counts)]}
    m = X[:, j] <= t
    return {"j": j, "t": t, "left": grow(X[m], y[m], classes, depth + 1, max_depth),
            "right": grow(X[~m], y[~m], classes, depth + 1, max_depth)}

def predict_one(node, x):
    while "leaf" not in node:
        node = node["left"] if x[node["j"]] <= node["t"] else node["right"]
    return node["leaf"]

from sklearn.datasets import load_wine
wine = load_wine()
Xw, yw, names = wine.data, wine.target, wine.feature_names
tree_mine = grow(Xw, yw, np.unique(yw), 0, 3)
tree_sk = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit(Xw, yw)
pm = np.array([predict_one(tree_mine, x) for x in Xw])
print(f"root split: ours '{names[tree_mine['j']]} <= {tree_mine['t']:.3f}', "
      f"scikit-learn '{names[tree_sk.tree_.feature[0]]} <= {tree_sk.tree_.threshold[0]:.3f}'")
print(f"identical predictions on the training data: {np.array_equal(pm, tree_sk.predict(Xw))}")
print(export_text(tree_sk, feature_names=list(names), decimals=2))
```

The rules printed by `export_text` are the whole model: three questions at
most lead to a cultivar. scikit-learn also considers the features in a random
order and breaks ties between equally good splits accordingly
(`random_state`); with real-valued features exact ties are rare, and our
greedy search finds the same tree.

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-mla7-trees-easy}
## Easy — three impurities, two splits
For the node and the two candidate splits of @exm-tree-hand, compute the
decrease of the entropy and of the misclassification impurity. Do the three
criteria agree? Then consider a node with 400 A and 400 B and the splits
(300 A, 100 B | 100 A, 300 B) and (200 A, 400 B | 200 A, 0 B): which does each
criterion prefer?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Write a small function for each impurity and apply @eq-tree-gain. The second
example is the classic one of @hastie2009, §9.2.3.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#fa6f354b .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def entropy(c):
    p = c / c.sum(); p = p[p > 0]
    return -(p * np.log2(p)).sum()
miscl = lambda c: 1 - c.max() / c.sum()
gini1 = lambda c: 1 - ((c / c.sum()) ** 2).sum()
def decrease(I, parent, left, right):
    n = parent.sum()
    return I(parent) - left.sum() / n * I(left) - right.sum() / n * I(right)
cases = {"example, split 1": ([6, 4], [5, 1], [1, 3]), "example, split 2": ([6, 4], [3, 0], [3, 4]),
         "800, split a": ([400, 400], [300, 100], [100, 300]), "800, split b": ([400, 400], [200, 400], [200, 0])}
for name, (p, l, r) in cases.items():
    p, l, r = (np.array(v, float) for v in (p, l, r))
    print(f"{name:17s} Gini {decrease(gini1, p, l, r):.3f}  entropy {decrease(entropy, p, l, r):.3f}  misclassification {decrease(miscl, p, l, r):.3f}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```

example, split 2  Gini 0.137  entropy 0.281  misclassification 0.100
800, split a      Gini 0.125  entropy 0.189  misclassification 0.250
800, split b      Gini 0.167  entropy 0.311  misclassification 0.250
```
:::
:::


In the 10-example node, Gini and misclassification prefer split 1, while
entropy prefers split 2, which creates a pure child: the criteria can
disagree, and entropy rewards purity most. In the 800-example node
misclassification cannot distinguish the splits (both leave 200 errors), but
split b produces a **pure** node and Gini and entropy prefer it: a pure node needs no further splitting, which is what growing a
tree should reward. The flat parts of the misclassification impurity are the
reason it is not used for growing. A common slip is to forget the weights
$n_L/n$, $n_R/n$.
:::

::: {#exr-mla7-trees-medium}
## Medium — a regression stump from scratch
Write the best-split search for **regression** (impurity: mean squared
deviation) and check it against `DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=1)` on 200
noisy points of $y = \sin(2\pi x)$. Then plot the depth-1, depth-3 and
depth-8 regression trees: what kind of function does a regression tree fit?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
With prefix sums of $y$ and $y^2$ you get the sum of squared deviations on
each side in $O(1)$ per cut: $\sum(y - \bar y)^2 = \sum y^2 - (\sum y)^2/m$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#cell-fig-tree-regression .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor
r = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = np.sort(r.uniform(0, 1, 200)); yr = np.sin(2 * np.pi * x) + r.normal(0, 0.3, 200)
def best_regression_cut(x, y):
    o = np.argsort(x); xs, ys = x[o], y[o]
    s1, s2 = np.cumsum(ys)[:-1], np.cumsum(ys ** 2)[:-1]
    m = np.arange(1, len(ys))
    sse_left = s2 - s1 ** 2 / m
    sse_right = (ys ** 2).sum() - s2 - (ys.sum() - s1) ** 2 / (len(ys) - m)
    total = np.where(xs[1:] > xs[:-1], sse_left + sse_right, np.inf)
    i = int(np.argmin(total)); return (xs[i] + xs[i + 1]) / 2
stump = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=1).fit(x[:, None], yr)
print(f"our cut {best_regression_cut(x, yr):.5f}, scikit-learn {stump.tree_.threshold[0]:.5f}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.2))
ax.scatter(x, yr, s=8, color=mlalgbook.MUTED)
grid = np.linspace(0, 1, 1000)[:, None]
for depth, c in zip((1, 3, 8), mlalgbook.COLORS):
    ax.plot(grid, DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=depth).fit(x[:, None], yr).predict(grid), color=c, lw=1.5, label=f"depth {depth}")
ax.legend(); ax.set_xlabel("x"); ax.set_ylabel("y"); plt.show()
```

The cut points coincide. A regression tree fits a **step function**: each
leaf is a constant, the mean of its examples. Shallow trees are too coarse
(bias), deep ones fit individual noisy points (variance) — the same trade-off
as $k$ in $k$-NN, with the leaf size playing the role of $k$. A common bug in
the prefix-sum version is an off-by-one between the cut position and the
counts on each side.
:::

## Hard — a tree that people can read
On the wine data, fit a tree with `max_depth` chosen by 5-fold
cross-validation among $1, \dots, 8$ on a training split; print its rules;
report test accuracy and the confusion matrix; and rewrite the tree's first
two levels as a sentence a non-specialist could apply. Which features does it
use, and does that agree with `feature_importances_`?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
`GridSearchCV(DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0), {"max_depth": range(1, 9)})`;
`export_text(best, feature_names=...)`. Trees need no scaling — splits are
invariant to monotone transformations of a feature.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#d0c42d0c .cell execution_count=5}

from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Xw, yw, test_size=0.3, stratify=yw, random_state=0)
gs = GridSearchCV(DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0), {"max_depth": range(1, 9)},

print(f"chosen depth {gs.best_params_['max_depth']} (CV accuracy {gs.best_score_:.3f}); test accuracy {best_tree.score(Xte, yte):.3f}")
print(confusion_matrix(yte, best_tree.predict(Xte)))

The rules read like a checklist (e.g. "if the proline content is high, it is

tree as "interpretable".

## Controlling the complexity: pruning {#sec-tree-pruning}

Grown until its leaves are pure, a tree fits the training data perfectly
(unless identical inputs have different labels) and overfits. Two families of
remedies exist. **Pre-pruning** stops growth early: `max_depth`,
`min_samples_split`, `min_samples_leaf`, `max_leaf_nodes`,
`min_impurity_decrease`. It is simple, but greedy: a split that looks useless
can enable very useful ones below it (XOR again). **Post-pruning** grows a
large tree and then removes branches that do not pay for their complexity.

**Cost-complexity pruning** [@breiman1984, ch. 3] measures a tree $T$ by
$$
R_\alpha(T) = R(T) + \alpha\,|\tilde T| ,
$$ {#eq-tree-ccp}
where $R(T)$ is the training impurity summed over the leaves (weighted by the
fraction of examples in each) and $|\tilde T|$ the number of leaves; $\alpha
\ge 0$ prices each leaf. For each $\alpha$ there is a smallest subtree
$T(\alpha)$ of the full tree minimising $R_\alpha$, and as $\alpha$ grows
these subtrees are **nested** — each obtained from the previous one by
collapsing branches — a result of Breiman and colleagues that we use without
proof. The sequence is computed by the **weakest-link** rule.

::: {#prp-tree-weakest-link}
## When a branch is worth keeping
Let $t$ be an internal node, $T_t$ the branch rooted at it, $R(t)$ the
impurity of $t$ if it were made a leaf, and $R(T_t)$ the summed impurity of
the branch's leaves. Collapsing $T_t$ into the leaf $t$ does not increase
$R_\alpha$ if and only if
$$
\alpha \ge g(t) = \frac{R(t) - R(T_t)}{|\tilde T_t| - 1} .
$$
The weakest link is the internal node with the smallest $g(t)$; pruning it
gives the next subtree of the sequence, at $\alpha = g(t)$.
:::

*In one line:* $g(t)$ is the impurity a branch removes per extra leaf it
costs; as the price per leaf rises, the branches that buy the least
improvement per leaf are cut first.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-tree-weakest-link
Collapsing $T_t$ changes only the part of $R_\alpha$ due to the branch: before,
$R(T_t) + \alpha|\tilde T_t|$; after, $R(t) + \alpha\cdot1$. The collapse does
not increase $R_\alpha$ iff $R(t) + \alpha \le R(T_t) + \alpha|\tilde T_t|$,
i.e. $\alpha(|\tilde T_t| - 1) \ge R(t) - R(T_t)$, which is the claim
(an internal node's branch has at least two leaves). Raising $\alpha$ from 0,
the first collapse that becomes worthwhile is at the smallest $g(t)$.
$\blacksquare$
:::

scikit-learn computes the sequence with `cost_complexity_pruning_path` and
prunes with `ccp_alpha`; $\alpha$ is then chosen by cross-validation like any
penalty. The widget shows the simpler pre-pruning knob, the depth, on a
two-class problem.

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-mla7-pruning-easy}
## Easy — the weakest link by hand
A tree has two internal nodes. Node $a$ (the root) has impurity $R(a) = 0.30$
as a leaf; its full branch has 4 leaves with total impurity $0.06$. Node $b$,
a child of $a$, has $R(b) = 0.12$ as a leaf and its branch has 2 leaves with
total $0.08$. Compute $g(a)$ and $g(b)$. Which node is pruned first, and at
which $\alpha$? Which tree is optimal for $\alpha = 0.05$?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
$g(t) = (R(t) - R(T_t))/(|\tilde T_t| - 1)$. After pruning $b$, recompute
$g(a)$ for the smaller tree.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
$g(a) = (0.30 - 0.06)/3 = 0.08$; $g(b) = (0.12 - 0.08)/1 = 0.04$. Node $b$
is pruned first, at $\alpha = 0.04$. The tree then has 3 leaves with total
impurity $0.06 - 0.08 + 0.12 = 0.10$, and $g(a) = (0.30 - 0.10)/2 = 0.10$. For
$\alpha = 0.05$ the optimal subtree is the 3-leaf tree ($b$ pruned, $a$
kept); $a$ is pruned only for $\alpha \ge 0.10$.

::: {#19ab15a2 .cell execution_count=7}
``` {.python .cell-code}
for name, (R_leaf, R_branch, leaves) in {"a": (0.30, 0.06, 4), "b": (0.12, 0.08, 2), "a after b": (0.30, 0.10, 3)}.items():
    print(name, round((R_leaf - R_branch) / (leaves - 1), 3))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
a 0.08
b 0.04
a after b 0.1
```
:::
:::


Note that $g(a)$ changes after $b$ is pruned: the weakest-link values must be
recomputed along the sequence. A frequent slip is to divide by the number of
leaves instead of the number of leaves minus one.
:::

::: {#exr-mla7-pruning-medium}
## Medium — choosing `ccp_alpha` by cross-validation
On the breast-cancer data (training split), compute the pruning path of a full
tree, choose `ccp_alpha` by 5-fold cross-validation over the path's values, and
compare test accuracy and number of leaves with the unpruned tree and with the
best `max_depth`.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
`DecisionTreeClassifier().cost_complexity_pruning_path(X, y).ccp_alphas`
gives the breakpoints; drop the last one (it prunes to the root).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#b7de8a64 .cell execution_count=8}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
Xb, yb = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
Xb_tr, Xb_te, yb_tr, yb_te = train_test_split(Xb, yb, test_size=0.3, stratify=yb, random_state=0)
alphas = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0).cost_complexity_pruning_path(Xb_tr, yb_tr).ccp_alphas[:-1]
cv5 = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
by_alpha = GridSearchCV(DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0), {"ccp_alpha": alphas}, cv=cv5).fit(Xb_tr, yb_tr)
by_depth = GridSearchCV(DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0), {"max_depth": range(1, 12)}, cv=cv5).fit(Xb_tr, yb_tr)
full = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0).fit(Xb_tr, yb_tr)
for name, m in (("unpruned", full), (f"ccp_alpha = {by_alpha.best_params_['ccp_alpha']:.4f}", by_alpha.best_estimator_),
                (f"max_depth = {by_depth.best_params_['max_depth']}", by_depth.best_estimator_)):
    print(f"{name:22s}: {m.get_n_leaves():3d} leaves, test accuracy {m.score(Xb_te, yb_te):.3f}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
unpruned              :  16 leaves, test accuracy 0.906
ccp_alpha = 0.0196    :   4 leaves, test accuracy 0.901
max_depth = 4         :  12 leaves, test accuracy 0.906
```
:::
:::


Pruning removes most of the leaves at little or no cost in accuracy; the
pruned and the depth-limited trees perform similarly here, the pruned one
usually with fewer leaves because it keeps depth only where it pays. With a
test set of 171 cases, differences of one or two points are within noise.
Mistake to avoid: choosing $\alpha$ on the test set — the path offers many
candidates, and the best on the test set is optimistic.
:::

::: {#exr-mla7-pruning-hard}
## Hard — how unstable is a tree?
Draw 50 bootstrap samples of the wine data, fit a tree of depth 3 to each, and
record the feature used at the root and the test accuracy on the out-of-bag
wines. How many different root features appear? How much does the accuracy
vary? Relate this to the variance term of @thm-bias-variance.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
A bootstrap sample draws $n$ indices with replacement; the out-of-bag examples
are those never drawn. `tree_.feature[0]` is the root feature.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#129eec28 .cell execution_count=9}
``` {.python .cell-code}
r = np.random.default_rng(1)
roots, accs = [], []
for b in range(50):
    idx = r.integers(0, len(yw), len(yw)); oob = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(len(yw)), idx)
    t = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit(Xw[idx], yw[idx])
    roots.append(names[t.tree_.feature[0]]); accs.append(t.score(Xw[oob], yw[oob]))
print(pd.Series(roots).value_counts().to_string())
print(f"out-of-bag accuracy: mean {np.mean(accs):.3f}, standard deviation {np.std(accs):.3f}, range {min(accs):.3f}–{max(accs):.3f}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
proline                         21
color_intensity                 13
flavanoids                      11
od280/od315_of_diluted_wines     3
alcohol                          2
out-of-bag accuracy: mean 0.896, standard deviation 0.051, range 0.769–1.000
```
:::
:::


Several different features appear at the root, and with them different trees
and different rules; the accuracy varies by many points from one sample to
the next. A small change in the data changes the first split, and the change
propagates to everything below it: trees are **high-variance** learners. That
is a disaster for interpretation ("the key measurement is…" depends on the
sample) and an opportunity for prediction: averaging many such trees reduces
the variance — the subject of the next section.
:::

## Bagging {#sec-tree-bagging}

The bias–variance decomposition (@thm-bias-variance) suggests a cure for
high-variance learners: average many of them. With one data set, Breiman's
**bootstrap aggregating** (bagging) [@breiman1996] simulates many training
sets by **bootstrap sampling** — drawing $n$ examples *with replacement* from
the $n$ available [@efron1979] — fits one tree per sample, and averages their
predictions (or takes the majority vote).

::: {#prp-tree-bootstrap}
## The out-of-bag fraction
In a bootstrap sample of size $n$, a given example is absent with probability
$(1 - 1/n)^n$, which increases to $e^{-1} \approx 0.368$ as $n \to \infty$.
:::

*In one line:* each tree sees about 63 % of the distinct examples; the other
37 % are a free validation set for that tree.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @prp-tree-bootstrap
Each of the $n$ independent draws misses the example with probability $1 -
1/n$, so all of them miss it with probability $(1 - 1/n)^n$. Taking logs,
$n\ln(1 - 1/n) = -1 - \frac{1}{2n} - \frac{1}{3n^2} - \dots$ (series of
$\ln(1 - u)$), which increases to $-1$. $\blacksquare$
:::

Predicting each training example with only the trees that did not see it
gives the **out-of-bag** (OOB) estimate of the error — an almost free
alternative to cross-validation (`oob_score=True`) [@breiman1996oob]. Why
does averaging help, and how much?

::: {#thm-tree-average-variance}
## The variance of an average of correlated predictors
Let $f_1, \dots, f_B$ be identically distributed random variables (the
predictions of $B$ trees at a point) with variance $\sigma^2$ and pairwise
correlation $\rho$. Then
$$
\operatorname{Var}\Big(\frac1B\sum_{b=1}^Bf_b\Big) = \rho\sigma^2 + \frac{1 - \rho}{B}\sigma^2 ,
$$
while the mean, and therefore the bias, is that of a single $f_b$.
:::

*In one line:* averaging removes the independent part of the trees'
fluctuations as $B$ grows, but not the part they share; the floor is
$\rho\sigma^2$ — so to gain more, make the trees less correlated.

::: {.deep kind="proof"}
## Proof of @thm-tree-average-variance
$\operatorname{Var}(\sum_bf_b) = \sum_b\operatorname{Var}f_b +
\sum_{b\ne c}\operatorname{Cov}(f_b, f_c) = B\sigma^2 + B(B - 1)\rho\sigma^2$.
Dividing by $B^2$: $\frac{\sigma^2}{B} + \frac{B-1}{B}\rho\sigma^2 = \rho\sigma^2
+ \frac{1 - \rho}{B}\sigma^2$. The mean of the average is the common mean
$\mathbb{E}f_b$ by linearity [@hastie2009, §15.2]. $\blacksquare$
:::

Bagging therefore helps unstable, low-bias learners — deep trees — and does
little for stable ones such as linear models. The simulation below estimates
bias² and variance of a deep regression tree and of bagged trees, as in
@fig-bias-variance.

::: {#cell-fig-tree-bagging-bv .cell execution_count=10}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from sklearn.ensemble import BaggingRegressor
r = np.random.default_rng(2)
truth = lambda x: np.sin(2 * np.pi * x)
x0 = np.linspace(0.02, 0.98, 200)[:, None]
Bs = [1, 2, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100]
preds = {B: [] for B in Bs}
for s in range(200):
    xs_ = r.uniform(0, 1, 100); ys_ = truth(xs_) + r.normal(0, 0.3, 100)
    for B in Bs:
        m = DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=s) if B == 1 else BaggingRegressor(DecisionTreeRegressor(), n_estimators=B, random_state=s)
        preds[B].append(m.fit(xs_[:, None], ys_).predict(x0))
bias2 = [np.mean((np.mean(preds[B], 0) - truth(x0[:, 0])) ** 2) for B in Bs]
var = [np.mean(np.var(preds[B], 0)) for B in Bs]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.2))
ax.plot(Bs, var, marker="o", ms=4, label="variance"); ax.plot(Bs, bias2, marker="o", ms=4, label="bias²")
ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.set_xlabel("number of bagged trees B (B = 1: a single tree)"); ax.legend(); plt.show()
print("B:        ", Bs); print("variance: ", np.round(var, 4)); print("bias^2:   ", np.round(bias2, 4))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Squared bias and variance (averaged over 200 test inputs, 200 simulated training sets of 100 noisy points of a sine) of a fully grown regression tree and of bagging with B trees. Averaging leaves the bias essentially unchanged and removes most of the variance.](07-trees-forests_files/figure-html/fig-tree-bagging-bv-output-1.png){#fig-tree-bagging-bv}
:::

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
B:         [1, 2, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100]
variance:  [0.09   0.0657 0.0523 0.0476 0.0444 0.0432 0.0425]
bias^2:    [0.0005 0.0005 0.0004 0.0003 0.0003 0.0003 0.0003]
```
:::
:::


The variance falls quickly over the first few trees and then levels off at
the floor $\rho\sigma^2$ set by the correlation between trees grown on
overlapping bootstrap samples; the bias stays essentially where it was, close to
zero for these fully grown trees.

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-mla7-bagging-easy}
## Easy — two numbers to remember
(a) Compute $(1 - 1/n)^n$ for $n = 2, 10, 100, 10\,000$. (b) Trees with
$\sigma^2 = 1$ and $\rho = 0.3$: what is the variance of the average of 10,
100 and infinitely many trees? How many trees bring it within 5 % of the
floor?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Use @thm-tree-average-variance; the excess over the floor is $(1 - \rho)/B$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
(a) $0.25, 0.349, 0.366, 0.368$. (b) $0.3 + 0.7/B$: $0.37$, $0.307$, $0.3$.
Within 5 % of the floor means $0.7/B \le 0.015$, i.e. $B \ge 47$.

::: {#7f8f173b .cell execution_count=11}
``` {.python .cell-code}
print([round((1 - 1 / n) ** n, 4) for n in (2, 10, 100, 10_000)], [0.3 + 0.7 / B for B in (10, 100)], int(np.ceil(0.7 / 0.015)))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
[0.25, 0.3487, 0.366, 0.3679] [0.37, 0.307] 47
```
:::
:::


Beyond a few dozen trees, adding more changes almost nothing — more trees
never hurt accuracy, they only cost time. The correlation, not the number of
trees, sets the limit.
:::

::: {#exr-mla7-bagging-medium}
## Medium — bagging and OOB from scratch
Implement bagging of `DecisionTreeClassifier`s on the wine data (100 trees,
majority vote), compute its out-of-bag accuracy yourself, and compare with
`BaggingClassifier(oob_score=True)` and with 5-fold cross-validation.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
For each example, collect the votes of the trees for which it was out of bag.
A handful of examples may be in every bootstrap sample — with 100 trees the
chance is negligible, but guard against it.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#37cd45e8 .cell execution_count=12}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from sklearn.ensemble import BaggingClassifier
r = np.random.default_rng(3)
n, K, B = len(yw), 3, 100
votes = np.zeros((n, K))
for b in range(B):
    idx = r.integers(0, n, n); oob = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(n), idx)
    t = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=b).fit(Xw[idx], yw[idx])
    votes[oob, t.predict(Xw[oob])] += 1
has = votes.sum(1) > 0
oob_mine = np.mean(votes[has].argmax(1) == yw[has])
bag = BaggingClassifier(DecisionTreeClassifier(), n_estimators=B, oob_score=True, random_state=0).fit(Xw, yw)
cv_bag = cross_val_score(BaggingClassifier(DecisionTreeClassifier(), n_estimators=B, random_state=0), Xw, yw, cv=StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)).mean()
cv_tree = cross_val_score(DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0), Xw, yw, cv=StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)).mean()
print(f"OOB accuracy: ours {oob_mine:.3f} ({has.sum()} wines with OOB votes), BaggingClassifier {bag.oob_score_:.3f}; 5-fold CV {cv_bag:.3f}; single tree CV {cv_tree:.3f}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
OOB accuracy: ours 0.972 (178 wines with OOB votes), BaggingClassifier 0.961; 5-fold CV 0.955; single tree CV 0.927
```
:::
:::


Our OOB accuracy and scikit-learn's agree up to the randomness of the
bootstrap samples, and both are close to the cross-validated accuracy —
obtained here at the cost of one fit instead of five. Bagging is clearly more
accurate than a single tree. (scikit-learn averages the trees' class
*probabilities* rather than counting votes; with fully grown trees, whose
leaves are pure, the two coincide.)
:::

::: {#exr-mla7-bagging-hard}
## Hard — measuring the correlation between trees
On the breast-cancer data, estimate the floor of @thm-tree-average-variance:
fit 200 trees on bootstrap samples, and on a held-out set compute, for each
point, the variance of the trees' predicted probabilities and the average
pairwise correlation between trees across points. Repeat for random forests
with `max_features` $= 1, 5, 30$ (all features = bagging). Which setting gives
the least correlated trees, and is it the most accurate?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
`RandomForestClassifier(max_features=m, n_estimators=200).estimators_` gives
the trees; stack their `predict_proba(X)[:, 1]` into a $200 \times n$ matrix and
use `np.corrcoef` on it (rows = trees). Bagging is `max_features=None` (or 30).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#0c989fa4 .cell execution_count=13}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
for m in (1, 5, 30):
    rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, max_features=m, random_state=0).fit(Xb_tr, yb_tr)
    P = np.stack([t.predict_proba(Xb_te)[:, 1] for t in rf.estimators_])      # trees x points
    C = np.corrcoef(P); rho = C[np.triu_indices_from(C, 1)].mean()
    print(f"max_features = {m:2d}: mean correlation between trees {rho:.3f}, mean per-point variance {P.var(0).mean():.4f}, "
          f"test accuracy {rf.score(Xb_te, yb_te):.3f}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
max_features =  1: mean correlation between trees 0.705, mean per-point variance 0.0693, test accuracy 0.936
max_features =  5: mean correlation between trees 0.794, mean per-point variance 0.0486, test accuracy 0.953
max_features = 30: mean correlation between trees 0.828, mean per-point variance 0.0408, test accuracy 0.924
```
:::
:::


Fewer candidate features per split make the trees less correlated — and each
tree individually worse (more variance per tree). The ensemble's accuracy
balances the two: very small `max_features` decorrelates the trees but makes
them weak; all features (bagging) makes them strong but similar. An
intermediate value, such as $\sqrt{30} \approx 5$, is usually best. This is
the trade-off random forests tune, and the topic of the next section.
:::

## Random forests {#sec-tree-forest}

Bagged trees are correlated because they are grown from similar samples with
the same greedy rule: a strong feature is chosen at the root of almost every
tree. Breiman's **random forest** [@breiman2001rf] adds a second source of
randomness: at **each split**, only a random subset of `max_features`
features is considered. Strong features are then sometimes unavailable, other
features get their chance, the trees become more diverse, $\rho$ falls, and by
@thm-tree-average-variance so does the variance of the average — usually more
than the individual trees get worse.

In scikit-learn, `RandomForestClassifier` uses `max_features="sqrt"` by
default ($\lfloor\sqrt d\rfloor$ candidates per split) and fully grown trees;
`RandomForestRegressor` uses all features (`max_features=1.0`), i.e. bagging,
by default. The main knobs are `n_estimators` (more is never worse, only
slower), `max_features`, and the leaf size (`min_samples_leaf`), which
smooths each tree. Forests need no scaling, handle interactions naturally,
and give an OOB estimate for free. The widget shows a forest's decision
regions as trees are added.

### Feature importance

Forests are less readable than a single tree, so they are often summarised by
**feature importances**. Two definitions are common, and they can disagree.

- **Mean decrease in impurity** (MDI, `feature_importances_`): the total
  impurity decrease @eq-tree-gain brought by the splits on each feature,
  weighted by the fraction of examples reaching them, averaged over the trees
  and normalised to sum to one. It is free, but computed on the **training**
  data, and it is biased towards features with many possible split points —
  continuous or high-cardinality features, even pure noise [@strobl2007].
- **Permutation importance** (`sklearn.inspection.permutation_importance`):
  the drop in a score on **held-out** data when one feature's values are
  randomly shuffled, breaking its link with the target [@breiman2001rf]. It
  measures what the model actually uses to predict new data, at the cost of
  extra predictions; with strongly correlated features it understates both
  (each can stand in for the other).

::: {#cell-fig-tree-importance .cell execution_count=15}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
rn = np.random.default_rng(4)
n_imp = 1000
binary, levels, noise = rn.integers(0, 2, n_imp), rn.integers(0, 4, n_imp), rn.uniform(size=n_imp)
p_true = 0.2 + 0.6 * binary + 0.05 * (levels - 1.5)                  # the noise feature plays no role
y_imp = (rn.random(n_imp) < p_true).astype(int)
X_imp = np.column_stack([binary, levels, noise]); fnames = ["binary (strong)", "4 levels (weak)", "continuous noise"]
Xi_tr, Xi_te, yi_tr, yi_te = train_test_split(X_imp, y_imp, test_size=0.5, stratify=y_imp, random_state=0)
rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0).fit(Xi_tr, yi_tr)
mdi = pd.Series(rf.feature_importances_, index=fnames)
perm = pd.Series(permutation_importance(rf, Xi_te, yi_te, n_repeats=20, random_state=0).importances_mean, index=fnames)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 2.6), sharey=True)
for ax, (title, s_), c in zip(axes, (("MDI (training data)", mdi), ("permutation (held-out data)", perm)), mlalgbook.COLORS):
    ax.barh(s_.index[::-1], s_.values[::-1], color=c); ax.set_title(title)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print("MDI:", ", ".join(f"{k} {v:.3f}" for k, v in mdi.items()))
print("permutation:", ", ".join(f"{k} {v:.3f}" for k, v in perm.items()), f"| test accuracy {rf.score(Xi_te, yi_te):.3f}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display}
![Feature importances of a random forest on synthetic data in which the label depends strongly on a binary feature, weakly on a four-level feature, and not at all on a continuous noise feature. Impurity-based importance (MDI, training data) ranks the noise first; permutation importance on held-out data ranks it near zero.](07-trees-forests_files/figure-html/fig-tree-importance-output-1.png){#fig-tree-importance}
:::

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
MDI: binary (strong) 0.433, 4 levels (weak) 0.029, continuous noise 0.538
permutation: binary (strong) 0.204, 4 levels (weak) 0.026, continuous noise 0.014 | test accuracy 0.712
```
:::
:::


The fully grown trees use the continuous noise feature to fit the label noise
of the training data — it offers hundreds of possible thresholds, the binary
feature only one — and MDI, computed on those same training data, credits it
with the largest share. On held-out data, shuffling the noise feature barely
changes the accuracy. Neither number is a causal effect; both describe a
model. When the question is "which measurements does the classifier rely on
for new data?", permutation importance on held-out data is the more
trustworthy answer [@molnar2022, §8.5].

::: {.deep}
## Beyond bagging: boosting
Bagging and random forests reduce variance by averaging independent-ish
trees. **Boosting** builds trees sequentially, each fitted to the errors of
the current ensemble, and mainly reduces **bias**: AdaBoost [@freund1997] and
gradient boosting [@friedman2001] (in scikit-learn
`HistGradientBoostingClassifier`) are often the most accurate models on
tabular data. They are not part of this course's syllabus; @hastie2009, ch. 10
develops them in the same spirit as this chapter.
:::

### Practice {.unnumbered}

::: {#exr-mla7-forest-easy}
## Easy — how many candidates?
With 30 features, how many candidate features does a split of
`RandomForestClassifier` consider by default? What is the probability that a
given feature is among them? With 5 features?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
$\lfloor\sqrt{d}\rfloor$ features drawn without replacement: a given feature
is included with probability $\lfloor\sqrt d\rfloor/d$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
$d = 30$: $\lfloor\sqrt{30}\rfloor = 5$ candidates, each feature included with
probability $5/30 \approx 0.167$. $d = 5$: $\lfloor\sqrt5\rfloor = 2$
candidates, probability $2/5 = 0.4$.

::: {#850d2b57 .cell execution_count=16}
``` {.python .cell-code}
print([(d, int(np.sqrt(d)), round(int(np.sqrt(d)) / d, 3)) for d in (30, 5)])
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
[(30, 5, 0.167), (5, 2, 0.4)]
```
:::
:::


With five features — the size of the fruit table — a strong feature is
unavailable at 60 % of the splits, so the forest is pushed to use the others:
a substantial decorrelation even with few features. Note that if none of the
drawn candidates gives a valid split, scikit-learn keeps drawing beyond
`max_features`.
:::

::: {#exr-mla7-forest-medium}
## Medium — is the OOB estimate honest?
On the wine data, compare for `RandomForestClassifier` with $n_{\text{est}} =
10, 50, 200, 500$ the OOB accuracy with the repeated 5-fold CV accuracy. When
are they close, and why can the OOB estimate be pessimistic with few trees?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
With few trees, each example is out of bag for only about $0.37\,n_{\text{est}}$
trees, so its OOB prediction comes from a small forest.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#f4dc44ed .cell execution_count=17}
``` {.python .cell-code}
import warnings
from sklearn.model_selection import RepeatedStratifiedKFold
cvr = RepeatedStratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, n_repeats=3, random_state=0)
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore", UserWarning)                     # few trees: some points have no OOB prediction
    for n_est in (10, 50, 200, 500):
        rf_ = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=n_est, oob_score=True, random_state=0).fit(Xw, yw)
        cvs = cross_val_score(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=n_est, random_state=0), Xw, yw, cv=cvr).mean()
        print(f"{n_est:3d} trees: OOB {rf_.oob_score_:.3f}, repeated 5-fold CV {cvs:.3f}")
```

prediction comes from only three or four trees — a much weaker forest than the
10-tree forest being evaluated — so the OOB estimate is pessimistic, and a
few wines may get no OOB prediction at all. Use OOB with a few hundred trees,
where it is a cheap substitute for cross-validation; for comparisons across
model families, use the same cross-validation folds for every model.
:::

::: {#exr-mla7-forest-hard}
## Hard — a forest among the other models
On the wine data, compare by nested cross-validation (same outer folds for
all) a random forest (tuning `max_features` $\in \{1, 2, 3, 6, 13\}$ and
`min_samples_leaf` $\in \{1, 3, 5\}$), $k$-NN with scaling (tuning $k$), an RBF
SVM with scaling (tuning $C$ and $\gamma$), Gaussian naive Bayes and a single
tuned tree. Report means ± standard errors. Then, for the forest fitted on a
training split, report the permutation importances on the test split. Which
measurements matter, and do the models agree on the difficulty of the
problem?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Hint
Build a dictionary of `GridSearchCV` objects (naive Bayes needs no tuning) and
loop over them with `cross_val_score` and the same `outer` splitter. Keep
`n_estimators` fixed (e.g. 300): it is not a parameter to tune.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#c74cb02e .cell execution_count=18}
``` {.python .cell-code}
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB
inner = StratifiedKFold(3, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
outer = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=1)
contenders = {
    "random forest": GridSearchCV(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0),
                                  {"max_features": [1, 2, 3, 6, 13], "min_samples_leaf": [1, 3, 5]}, cv=inner),
    "k-NN": GridSearchCV(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier()), {"kneighborsclassifier__n_neighbors": list(range(1, 31, 2))}, cv=inner),
    "RBF SVM": GridSearchCV(make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC()), {"svc__C": np.logspace(-1, 2, 4), "svc__gamma": np.logspace(-3, 0, 4)}, cv=inner),
    "Gaussian naive Bayes": GaussianNB(),
    "single tree": GridSearchCV(DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0), {"max_depth": range(1, 9)}, cv=inner),
}
for name, m in contenders.items():
    s = cross_val_score(m, Xw, yw, cv=outer)
    print(f"{name:21s} {s.mean():.3f} ± {s.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(s)):.3f}")
rf_w = contenders["random forest"].fit(Xtr, ytr).best_estimator_
pi = permutation_importance(rf_w, Xte, yte, n_repeats=30, random_state=0)
print(pd.Series(pi.importances_mean, index=names).sort_values(ascending=False).head(5).round(3).to_string())
```

```
random forest         0.989 ± 0.007
k-NN                  0.977 ± 0.011
RBF SVM               0.983 ± 0.007
Gaussian naive Bayes  0.983 ± 0.011
single tree           0.921 ± 0.028
proline            0.042
color_intensity    0.035
alcohol            0.018
magnesium          0.011
total_phenols      0.009
```
:::
:::


The forest, $k$-NN, the SVM and naive Bayes all reach high accuracy on the
wine data, within a couple of standard errors of each other; the single tree
is clearly behind — the variance that the forest averages away. The
permutation importances single out a few measurements, which overlap with
those the single tree chose (@exr-mla7-trees-hard). When strong models of
very different kinds agree, the problem is easy for this representation of
the data, and the choice among them can be made on other grounds:
readability, prediction cost, robustness. Mistakes to avoid: tuning the
favourite model more generously than the others, and reporting importances
computed on the training data as if they described generalisation.
:::

::: {.project-link}
**In the project.** Trees and forests are natural comparison models for the
fruit classifier: they need **no scaling** (a split on grams is unaffected by
expressing them in kilograms), they handle interactions between
measurements, and a shallow tree turns the classification into rules an
operator can apply at the warehouse door. They also help with the
exploratory question of **which measurements separate which fruits**: if one
feature alone isolates a class, the root of a tree will find it immediately —
a strong hint to check whether that feature is genuine or an artefact of the
data. Use permutation importance on held-out data, not MDI, to say which
measurements the model relies on.
:::

## Common pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning}
## Watch out
- **Unconstrained trees**: perfect training accuracy, poor generalisation;
  prune or limit growth, or use a forest.
- **Interpreting one tree's structure** as a stable truth about the data: a
  different sample can give a different tree.
- **MDI importances** as evidence: they are biased towards continuous and
  high-cardinality features and computed on training data.
- **Tuning `n_estimators`**: more trees never hurt accuracy; tune
  `max_features` and the leaf size instead.
- **OOB with few trees**: pessimistic and incomplete.
- **Scaling "for safety"** before trees: harmless but useless; spend the
  effort on features.
- **Extrapolation**: trees predict constants outside the training range; a
  forest cannot predict beyond the largest training target.
:::

## Summary

- A tree splits on one feature at a time, greedily maximising the impurity
  decrease; Gini and entropy are strictly concave, so splits never increase
  them; leaves predict majorities or means.
- Complexity is controlled by pre-pruning parameters or by cost-complexity
  pruning, where a branch is kept iff $\alpha < (R(t) - R(T_t))/(|\tilde T_t| -
  1)$.
- Trees are low-bias, high-variance learners: small data changes reshape them.
- Bagging averages trees grown on bootstrap samples (each misses about $1/e$
  of the data, giving the OOB estimate); the variance of the average is $\rho
  \sigma^2 + (1 - \rho)\sigma^2/B$.
- Random forests also subsample features at each split, lowering $\rho$; they
  need little tuning; permutation importance on held-out data describes what
  they use.

## Exercises

::: {#exr-mla7-xor-tree}
**Greedy splitting and XOR.** Generate 400 points uniform in $[-1, 1]^2$ with
label $\mathbb{1}\{x_1x_2 > 0\}$. Fit trees of depth 1, 2 and 4 and report
their accuracies. Why does the depth-1 tree fail, and why does a depth-2 tree
still struggle although two splits suffice in principle?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution

::: {#74992681 .cell execution_count=19}
``` {.python .cell-code}
r = np.random.default_rng(5)
Xx = r.uniform(-1, 1, (400, 2)); yx = (Xx[:, 0] * Xx[:, 1] > 0).astype(int)
Xx_te = r.uniform(-1, 1, (4000, 2)); yx_te = (Xx_te[:, 0] * Xx_te[:, 1] > 0).astype(int)
for depth in (1, 2, 4):
    t = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=depth, random_state=0).fit(Xx, yx)
    print(f"depth {depth}: root split on x{t.tree_.feature[0] + 1} at {t.tree_.threshold[0]:+.3f}, test accuracy {t.score(Xx_te, yx_te):.3f}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
depth 1: root split on x1 at +0.586, test accuracy 0.494
depth 2: root split on x1 at +0.586, test accuracy 0.707
depth 4: root split on x1 at +0.586, test accuracy 0.994
```
:::
:::


Every single split leaves each side with about half of each class: no first
split reduces the impurity much, and the greedy rule picks a threshold
essentially at random — usually not at 0, where it should be. A depth-2 tree
then has the right structure only if the root happened to cut near 0; deeper
trees recover by cutting again. Greedy growth cannot see that a useless split
enables a perfect one below it — the limitation of pre-pruning noted in
@sec-tree-pruning.
:::

::: {#exr-mla7-monotone}
**Invariance to monotone transformations.** Show that replacing a feature $x_j$
by $\phi(x_j)$ with $\phi$ strictly increasing does not change the partition
of the training data produced by a tree (only the thresholds). Check it with
scikit-learn on the wine data using $\phi = \log$ on proline. What does this
imply for preprocessing before trees?
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Solution
A split $x_j \le t$ partitions the examples according to the order of their
$x_j$ values; a strictly increasing $\phi$ preserves that order, so every
partition reachable with $x_j$ is reachable with $\phi(x_j)$ (with threshold
between the images of the two neighbouring values) and the impurity of each
partition is unchanged. The greedy search therefore finds the same partitions.

::: {#7e74f94d .cell execution_count=20}
``` {.python .cell-code}
Xlog = Xw.copy(); Xlog[:, 12] = np.log(Xlog[:, 12])
t1 = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0).fit(Xw, yw); t2 = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0).fit(Xlog, yw)
print("same leaves for every training wine:", np.array_equal(t1.apply(Xw), t2.apply(Xlog)))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
same leaves for every training wine: True
```
:::
:::


Scaling, standardisation and monotone transformations (log, Box–Cox,
Yeo–Johnson) are pointless for trees and forests — unlike for $k$-NN, SVMs
and networks. (scikit-learn places thresholds at midpoints, so the thresholds
themselves differ, and on unseen data the two trees can disagree slightly.)
:::
